_comment: Rotation list for the proactive podcast researcher (scripts/podcast_researcher.py) and the podcast-deep-research workflow (.claude/workflows/podcast-deep-research.js). Each entry is one candidate episode topic. 'domain' defaults to 'medicine'; only medicine topics (with 'pubmed_query' feeding PubMed E-utilities) are eligible for the local PubMed fallback — non-medicine domains ('query' instead) are researched exclusively by the deep-research workflow with domain-appropriate lenses. 'debate' picks --format debate over deep-dive when the topic has genuine, citable controversy.

topics.title: The A&E Crisis — What's Happening to UK Emergency Departments
topics.query: UK A&E crisis emergency department crowding four hour standard exit block ambulance handover delays causes solutions
topics.angle: Answer four questions, in order, and let the sources rather than the hosts' priors decide each: (1) What is actually happening to UK EDs — the real numbers on four-hour performance, 12-hour DTA waits, ambulance handover delays, bed occupancy, and how they have moved over the last decade. (2) Why — the causal mechanism, distinguishing front-door demand from exit block and whole-system flow, and how much of the change each candidate cause actually accounts for. (3) How to fix it — named interventions with evidence behind them, separated clearly from interventions that are merely asserted, and who would have to act to deliver each. (4) Who is to blame — treat this as a genuine, contested question: lay out each camp's case (underfunding, social-care collapse, workforce attrition, primary-care access, trust-level flow and management, demographic demand, specific political decisions), give each its strongest advocate and its strongest critic, and be willing to conclude that the evidence points harder at some than others rather than distributing blame evenly for the sake of balance.

topics.title: Daily Bloods and the Daily CRP — Dismantling a Ward Ritual
topics.pubmed_query: C-reactive protein serial monitoring hospitalized OR repetitive laboratory testing inpatient low value
topics.angle: Test four independent arguments against daily CRP monitoring and let the sources decide each, rather than assuming the conclusion. (1) Kinetics: CRP's plasma half-life is fixed near 19 hours across health and every disease studied, so clearance carries no information and the plasma level is a pure readout of hepatic synthesis rate — which puts a hard ceiling of about 58% on any 24-hour fall, and places the peak 48 hours after the stimulus. (2) Measurement: within-subject biological variation is large enough that the smallest statistically detectable fall exceeds the largest physiologically possible one, so most day-to-day movement is noise; but be honest that these coefficients come from stable subjects and were never validated in acute illness. (3) Decision theory: a test is only worth ordering if some result would cross a threshold, and daily bloods are ordered with no threshold stated — note the asymmetry whereby the number escalates antibiotics but is never allowed to de-escalate them. (4) Randomised evidence: ADAPT-Sepsis mandated daily CRP across 41 NHS ICUs and changed antibiotic duration by 0.09 days while procalcitonin saved 0.88. Then steelman the practice properly — the iatrogenic anaemia case really is overstated, and the number does real work as medico-legal cover and as a handover token — and identify where serial CRP genuinely earns its keep (post-operative day 3-5 rule-out for anastomotic leak, point-of-care CRP in primary care, neonatal sepsis stopping rules), which in every case means one sample, biologically timed, against a threshold set in advance. Close on sampling interval and pre-stated thresholds, not on measuring less carefully.
